note:
Leviticus continues the narrative that concludes in Exodus with God coming to dwell in the midst of the Israelite camp. Of necessity, special arrangements need to be put in place for the Holy One to reside among the Israelites. Priority is given to outlining a range of sacrifices that address the serious consequences of human sin. The regulations are subdivided into sections addressed to the laity (1:1–6:7) and to the priests (6:8–7:38). Sacrifice in Israel involved the offering of selected domestic animals, grain, oil, and wine. In every animal offering the worshiper placed his hand on the victim’s head, thereby identifying himself with the animal, saying in effect, “This animal represents me.” The animal sacrifices involved the animal’s death, and so the sacrifices had atoning symbolism: the animal dying in the sinful worshiper’s place represented redemption from the death he deserved. There is then a common core of meaning and significance shared by all the sacrifices. But each sacrifice also had its own distinctive ritual features and religious emphases. This is indicated by the different names of the sacrifices, which sometimes highlight the ritual distinctiveness (“_burnt_ offering”) and sometimes the theologically distinctive feature (“_peace_ offering”).

Although the Lord, in response to Moses’s intercession (Ex. 32), had rescinded His verdict to judge the people for their idolatrous worship of the golden calf, their ongoing sin remained a problem. These sacrifices provided atonement for them.

**1:1 tent of meeting.** The tent shrine or tabernacle described in Ex. 26.

Israel must obey these divinely given instructions on how to be fit to live in the presence of God. God, not humans, prescribes the way His people must live with Him.

**of livestock.** Only unblemished (v. 3) domesticated animals can be offered. Wild animals, which cost nothing to the worshiper, cannot be offered.

The burnt offering, which begins the list of sacrifices, is the most comprehensive sacrifice. Its distinctive feature is that the whole animal, except for the skin, is burned on the altar. This symbolizes the total consecration of the worshiper to God’s service, and it serves to cover the sins of the worshiper (v. 4 and note). The regulations begin by specifying the most expensive kind of animal that could be offered, the bull (vv. 2–9), and end with the cheapest, the young pigeon (vv. 14–17). No Israelite is excluded from making a burnt offering because he is too poor.

**1:3 he shall offer.** The layman offering the sacrifice (vv. 4–6, 9) is to kill, skin, cut up, and wash the animal, whereas the priest brings it to God by putting the blood and flesh on the altar.

**entrance of the tent.** The screened-off courtyard surrounding the tabernacle of meeting. The great altar and a laver for washing the sacrifices stand in the courtyard (v. 9).
Lit. “to cover over.” The death of the animal in place of the sinner “covers over” or shields the worshiper from the holy wrath of God.

LORD **.** The meaning of this phrase is seen most clearly in Gen. 8:21. Sacrifices avert God’s anger, causing Him to look benevolently on the worshiper. God is holy and cannot look at sin. The phrase is anthropomorphic, describing in human language how the sacrifice is satisfying to the Lord. The NT speaks of the death of Christ in similar language (Eph. 5:2).
Sheep and goats are sacrificed in the same way as bulls in vv. 3–9.
A simpler procedure is prescribed for doves or pigeons, the offering of the poor. Due to the smaller size of the offering, the priest carries out the whole ceremony.

Usually offered in conjunction with an animal sacrifice, it consists of wheat flour mixed with olive oil, incense, and salt. The mixture is baked, fried, or, in the case of a grain offering of firstfruits, roasted (vv. 4–7, 14). Like the other sacrifices, the grain offering symbolizes the worshiper’s dedication of himself to God. The Hebrew name for this offering suggests that it was a gift, expressing the worshiper’s gratitude to God. This name is also used to describe tribute, which underscores the subservience of the presenter to someone greater (Gen. 32:13; Judg. 3:15; 2 Kin. 8:8).
Only a handful of the grain offering is burned; the rest goes to the priest (v. 3). Such offerings constitute an important part of a priest’s income.
Possibly omitted because they cause fermentation or decay, which suggests corruption.
Because salt is a preservative, it symbolizes the enduring covenant between God and Israel (Num. 18:19 note).
See 23:9–14; Deut. 26:1–11. The Israelite is expected to give the first of his harvest to God, and on this occasion the grain offering is prepared differently.

Also called the “fellowship offering.” The Hebrew name for this offering is related to the word _shalom,_ meaning “peace, well-being.” This sacrifice is unique in that the worshiper and his family can eat much of the meat, as only part of the offering is given to the priests or burned on the altar. It is a sacrifice brought when someone is seeking God’s blessing or celebrating blessings received. It is offered to underline a solemn prayer (such as a vow), when such a prayer is answered, or out of simple gratitude (7:16). Eating meat was a rare luxury in ancient times and was usually something of a celebration. Moses prescribes that every animal killed for food must be offered in sacrifice first (17:3 note), so at least during the wilderness period, every meal involving meat is preceded by a peace offering.
The choicest parts of the carcass are symbolically given to God by being burned., 4

The OT insists that God supplies man with food, not vice versa (Gen. 1:29; Ps. 50:12–14). Therefore, this comment must be understood figuratively—God is pleased with the sacrifice offered in faith (cf. Heb. 11:4), just as human beings enjoy food.

Fat from sacrificial animals belongs to God (v. 3). Eating blood means eating meat from which the blood has not been drained (1 Sam. 14:33). The theological reason for this ban is given in 17:11 (see Gen. 9:4 and note).

With the words “If anyone sins” (4:2), Moses introduces his instruction to the laity regarding the sin or purification offering. While most sacrifices make atonement for sin to some extent, purification is the dominant concern of the sin offering. Sin and uncleanness make a person unfit to be in God’s presence and also pollute the sanctuary, making it impossible for God to dwell there. The sin offering is designed to cope with this aspect of sin by purifying the sanctuary. The distinctive feature of the sin offering is the use to which the sacrificial blood is put. In other sacrifices the animal’s blood is splashed over the side of the altar, but in the case of the sin offering it can be applied to the horned corners of the altar, or sprinkled inside the tabernacle tent (on the incense altar or veil) or even inside the Most Holy Place. The greater the sin, the greater the defilement caused within the sanctuary. Because the tabernacle and its furniture were closely associated with the people who met God there (Heb. 9:22 note), the people’s sin defiled the tabernacle. Such pollution required cleansing.

These verses deal with four cases where people of various ranks do something sinful “unintentionally” (v. 2 text note): the high priest (vv. 3–12), the congregation (vv. 13–21), a ruler (vv. 22–26), and a common person (vv. 27–35).

The high priest. His sin has the direct consequence of “bringing guilt on the people” and requires the most expensive atonement, a bull.

**he shall offer.** The sin (or purification) and guilt (or reparation) offerings were compulsory after committing certain sins, whereas the other offerings could sometimes be offered voluntarily when the worshiper felt so inclined.
The serious effects of high priestly sin are shown by the need to purify “the veil of the sanctuary” (the veil separating the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place, Ex. 26:31–35).

This piece of sacred furniture stands in front of the curtain leading into the Most Holy Place. It is cleansed by sprinkling with blood, the holy cleansing agent, making it possible for God to dwell in the tent.

See Heb. 13:11–13 and notes.

**a clean place.** Many places outside the camp contained impurity that would make the priest unfit to officiate in worship. He was to avoid these and put the ashes left from the burnt offering in a designated clean place, where the remainder of the sacrificial bull was burned.
For sin involving the congregation as a whole, a procedure like the one described in vv. 3–12 is prescribed, with the community elders representing the people at the altar (v. 15).

A sin by a leader of a tribe or clan is not as serious a threat to the tabernacle’s holiness as the first two cases (vv. 3–21). This is reflected in that he is required to offer only a male goat (v. 23), whose blood is applied not within the tent, but outside to the altar of burnt offering (v. 25).
Unintentional sins by ordinary Israelites are treated similarly to those of leaders. However, they can offer a female goat instead of a male goat, and if they are poor, birds or grain (5:7–13).

It is debated whether this section belongs with what precedes (the sin offering, ch. 4) or with what follows (the guilt offering, 5:14–6:7). Because of the similarity of 4:1 and 5:14, as well as the occurrence of the Hebrew term for “sin offering” throughout 4:1–5:13, many argue that the description of the guilt offering begins at 5:14. Alternatively, the occurrence of the Hebrew word _asham_ (meaning “guilt” or “guilt offering”) in 5:6, 7 has led some to conclude that the discussion of the guilt offering begins in 5:1.

**5:1–6** These verses treat sins of omission, inadvertence, or rashness. The cases in view are (a) the sin of withholding evidence (v. 1); (b) the sin of contact with anything unclean (vv. 2, 3); and (c) the sin of careless oath-taking (v. 4).
See notes regarding cleanness and uncleanness on chs. 11–16.
These sins require confession to God in the presence of a priest and a sin offering for the forgiveness of the sinner (cf. 1 John 1:7, 9).
The poor man’s sin offering is like the humblest burnt offering (1:14–17), except for the sprinkling of the blood (5:9; cf. 1:15).
See “Atonement” at Rom. 3:25.
The items brought here as sin offerings resemble those of the grain offering of ch. 2, but no oil or incense is included.

Moses gives instructions to the laity regarding the guilt or reparation offering. While the focus of the sin offering is upon purification of the sanctuary, the guilt offering is concerned with restitution or reparation. Three types of sins requiring guilt offerings are mentioned: misuse of “the holy things of the LORD” (5:15, 16), supposed sin involving things that “ought not to be done” (5:17–19), and trespasses against a neighbor’s rights and property (6:2–7).

A reference to tithes and offerings, as well as property dedicated to God (22:7, 10, 14; 27:28).

**add a fifth.** In cases where a guilt or reparation offering is required, misappropriated property also has to be restored plus a fifth (cf. 6:5). This is intended to compensate the wronged party.

As the phrase “though he did not know it” (v. 17) indicates, these verses concern the person who suspects he has transgressed against divine law or another person but is not sure. Sacrificial remedy is provided for those with an uneasy conscience and reparation is offered to God.
Trespasses against a neighbor require restoration of the loss plus “a fifth” (v. 5), and the offering of sacrifice to God (cf. Matt. 5:24).
Having addressed the laity concerning the laws of sacrifice, Moses now addresses the priests, especially about their entitlement to a share in the sacrifices.

See note on 1:3–17. The consecration portrayed by the burnt offering points to Christ, who is wholly consecrated to God, suffering death for sin and bringing about the believer’s death to sin (cf. Rom. 6:2–7).
Being white, this apparel probably symbolizes purity. These garments are to cover their private parts (see Ex. 20:26; 28:42 note; cf. Gen. 3:7, 21).

This action is perhaps prescribed as a reminder of God’s continual presence and the people’s need for continual atonement. The first burnt offering at the tabernacle is consumed by fire from God Himself (9:24).

This is a warning to laity not to touch food consecrated to God in sacrifice. Contact with the sacred food would render a person ritually holy (v. 27 text note; Ex. 29:37). Those who incurred such holiness probably were temporarily placed under restrictions like those governing the activity of priests (21:1–8).
The priest’s grain offering, mentioned here for the first time, had to be offered daily (6:20). Unlike these daily sacrifices, Christ our great High Priest offered Himself “once for all” (Heb. 7:27).
The high priest.
See 4:1–5:13 and notes.
See 5:14–6:7 and notes.

See note on 3:1. Here rules are given about the grain offerings that must accompany peace offerings, and how the meat must be eaten (vv. 15, 16). As the only offering in which the worshiper receives back a portion of the sacrifice, the peace offering involves a fellowship meal eaten in the presence of God. This aspect of the meal is reflected in the Lord’s Supper, wherein believers eat of the sign and seal of Christ’s sacrifice in fellowship with God and one another.

The Hebrew word here translated “thanksgiving” can also mean “confession” (of sin or of faith in response to God’s goodness and mercy). The sacrifice serves to underline prayers for forgiveness and healing, or as an expression of gratitude for prayers answered.

People in dire straits might make vows promising something to God if He will answer their prayers (Gen. 28:20–22; 1 Sam. 1:11; 2:21). Such vows are usually accompanied by a peace offering when first made and then again when the vows are fulfilled.

**freewill offering.** This spontaneous offering showed gratitude to God.

See notes regarding cleanness and uncleanness on chs. 11–16.

**be cut off.** This language is a general expression for coming under God’s curse, the exact meaning of which is determined by the context of Scripture. It may mean the penalty of execution (e.g., Ex. 31:14–15) or of death without children (18:29; cf. 20:20). In any event, God puts the offender to death with or without human agency.
This phrase refers to eating meat from which the blood has not been drained (1 Sam. 14:33). The reason for this ban is given in 17:11 and Gen. 9:4.

The Lord instructs Moses regarding the institution of the priesthood. The narrative moves from their installation (ch. 8), through their first sacrifices (ch. 9), to God’s judgment of two priests (ch. 10).

**8:1–36** The instructions of Ex. 29 for the consecration of the Aaronic priests are carried out. The repetition and elaborateness of the sacrifices (Ex. 29:35–37), and the splendor of Aaron’s apparel (vv. 7–9) all point to the importance of the high priesthood. He represents Israel before God.

verse_quote: at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
note: See note on 1:3.
See note on Ex. 28:6.
See note on Ex. 28:30.
Applying the blood to the different parts of Aaron’s body symbolized cleansing from the defilement caused by sin (Ex. 29:20 note).
The consecration of Aaron and his sons takes eight days and culminates in the offering of his first sacrifices and the appearance of God’s glory (9:23–24).
Aaron has to make atonement for himself first and then for the people (cf. Heb. 5:3).
The traditional priestly blessing is found in Num. 6:23–26.

LORD **.** God’s appearance signals His approval of the first sacrifices offered by the newly consecrated priests. The fire that then consumes the offering (v. 24) confirms God’s acceptance of Aaron’s ministry (cf. 1 Kin. 18:38; Heb. 12:28, 29).

The Lord, who accepted Aaron’s sacrifice (9:23, 24), now rejects the ministry of his sons Nadab and Abihu. His sons Eleazar and Ithamar fail in their first ministrations as well (vv. 16–20). These first halting steps of the Levites foreshadow their subsequent history and lead to Malachi’s prophecy of a purified priesthood (Mal. 3:1–5).

**10:1 censer.** A vessel for burning incense.

**unauthorized fire.** Lit. “strange fire.” Perhaps Nadab and Abihu had used coals from elsewhere than the altar (Lev. 16:12; cf. Ex. 30:1–9). Some interpreters suggest that the two men were also drunk, but this is not specifically stated (cf. v. 9). While the precise nature of Nadab and Abihu’s offering is unknown, they sought to draw near to the Lord by other means than those He had appointed.

verse_quote: fire came out from before the
note: LORD **.** The OT frequently warns people against approaching God in an unfit state (Ex. 19:12, 21); this principle is also evident in the NT (Acts 5:1–10; 1 Cor. 11:29, 30). Eating sacrificial food while unclean (7:21) or entering the Most Holy Place without divine approval might lead to death (16:2). The same divine fire that ignited the inaugural sacrifice, providing atonement for the people (9:24), now engulfs those who encroach upon His altar in an unautho­rized fashion. So also the same divine wrath against sin that fell upon Christ in His vicarious sacrifice for His people will blaze against those who reject that sacrifice and yet attempt to approach God in their sin (Heb. 10:26–31).
These were signs of mourning (13:45). The high priest is forbidden to mourn even their closest relatives (21:10–12), since total consecration to God means complete separation from death.

verse_quote: distinguish between the holy and the common.
note: The priest’s job is to teach the people these basic religious distinctions. “Holy” applies to what belongs to God, “clean” to what is fit for Him. See notes regarding cleanness and uncleanness on chs. 11–16.

Aaron and his sons had offered two sin offerings (v. 19; cf. 9:8–17): one for Aaron, the blood of which was sprinkled in the holy place and the remainder burned (4:6, 12), and one for the people, the blood of which was sprinkled on the altar of burnt offering in the courtyard and which was then to be eaten by the priests (6:25, 26). Normally he and his sons should have eaten the meat of the people’s sin offering to complete the atonement process, but they had not.

verse_quote: such things as these have happened to me.
note: Probably a reference to the terrifying events of vv. 1–7. After the display of God’s consuming judgment, Aaron is apparently afraid or too upset by the sudden death of his sons to eat the sacrificial meat, which is holy (6:26–29).
He realizes that the mistake of Aaron and his sons is not motivated by rebellion or by a disregard for the holiness of God.

In these chapters, Moses explains the difference between the ceremonially clean and unclean. For the Israelites, people, objects, places, and even time could be placed along a spectrum with holiness on one side and uncleanness on the other. Holiness is associated with God, for He alone is inherently holy. At the other extreme is uncleanness, associated with forces opposed to God. To be in God’s presence requires a person to be holy; sin causes him to be ritually unclean and means that he cannot come near God. Anyone who is unclean or who has come in contact with uncleanness is to abstain from public worship until he is cleansed. Because holiness is linked to God, it is associated with perfection and life. Uncleanness, in marked contrast, is linked to chaos and death. Normal, healthy creatures are clean, but abnormal or unhealthy creatures, and particularly corpses, are unclean. Abnormalities that suggest or that might lead to death are marks of uncleanness. Life and death are not to be mixed, so the unclean is never to enter God’s presence. Ultimately, it is Christ, the great Mediator and High Priest, who triumphs over death and corruption in behalf of those who trust in Him (1 Cor. 15:20–28, 50–57).

**11:1–47** Moses instructs the Israelites regarding the principles of cleanness, showing them that, though all corpses are unclean (vv. 24, 27, 31–40), some perfectly healthy creatures are also stated to be unclean in a milder sense and therefore must not be eaten. Although some of the forbidden animals posed a possible health threat (e.g., pigs as carriers of trichinosis), the classification of uncleanness is not based on health grounds. Rather, the principle teaches basic moral and spiritual truths. Carnivorous animals and birds of prey eat flesh with blood in it, something forbidden to human beings (7:26). Such animals also come into contact with carcasses, which are unclean. The clean creatures here symbolize Israelites, while unclean animals symbolize Gentiles. Only domesticated clean animals may be offered in sacrifice, for the sacrificial animal symbolizes the priest. In restricting his diet to clean animals, the Israelite was reminded that God had chosen Israel alone among the nations. Only when the new covenant admitted Gentiles to the community of God were the food laws abrogated (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15).
Cud-chewing, cloven-hoofed land animals are clean and so can be eaten. Other animals are unclean. Animals with claws are normally carnivorous.
Only ordinary fish with fins and scales are clean. Other water creatures are unclean and therefore inedible.
Birds of prey, associated with death, are unclean, but most other types of bird are clean.
Insects that hop may be eaten (v. 21), but not others.
See theological note “The Holiness of God.”

The word “holy” is often taken to mean “separate” or “set apart,” but it implies much more than simply being set apart. It is associated with wholeness and perfection. Only God is intrinsically holy. He is by nature majestic, awesome, pure, and perfect. He demonstrated His transcendent holiness by His creation of the world (see Gen. 1:1, 3 and notes), by His great acts in history such as redeeming His people from Egypt, and by His perfect laws. Israel’s holiness is derived from her unique covenant relationship with the only true and living God. His covenant provides, among other things, moral and judicial laws that reflect God’s own righteous standards, and the sacrificial system to atone for sin. The immediate background for this designation of Israel as a “holy nation” is the Lord’s appearance on Mount Sinai: they washed their clothes, avoided contact with the mountain, and abstained from sexual intercourse in preparation for that unique event (Ex. 19:10–15, 21–24; Heb. 12:18–21). By dwelling among the people, God makes them holy and demands that they be holy as He is holy (cf. 1 Pet. 1:16).

Jesus Christ, the Mediator of the new covenant (Heb. 8:6; 9:15; 12:24), also demands perfection (Matt. 5:48). But He provides the new Israel with holiness by His perfect sacrifice, which removed the sins of His people forever (Heb. 9; 10), and by His Holy Spirit, who inscribes God’s moral law on their hearts (2 Cor. 3:3; cf. Jer. 31:31–34). Without holiness, no one will see God (Heb. 12:14).

The flow of blood after childbirth makes a mother unclean (vv. 4, 5, 7). Loss of blood could lead to death, thus illustrating the equation of uncleanness with death or the threat thereof (chs. 11–16 note).

The text does not explain why the birth of a daughter made a mother unclean for twice as long as the birth of a son. Perhaps a daughter, as a potential mother and subject eventually to the loss of blood in childbirth, was subject to uncleanness in a way a son was not (12:2 note).
These sacrifices for atonement and purification are offered after the birth of Jesus (Luke 2:24).

These chapters contain God’s laws concerning unclean skin diseases referred to as “leprous disease” (13:2, 8). Modern physicians recognize here the symptoms of various modern complaints, but we should remember that the biblical classification is based primarily on spiritual rather than hygienic or medical considerations. The key principle in identifying a skin disease as “unclean” was whether the skin seemed to be rotting away, suggesting the spiritual principle of death. Patchy complaints amounted to uncleanness (vv. 9, 10), but a complaint affecting the whole body did not (vv. 12, 13). Stable conditions were clean, but deteriorating ones were unclean (vv. 5–8, 18–37). Similar principles applied to the diagnosis of uncleanness in clothing: progressive mildews were unclean (vv. 47–52), but stable ones were clean (vv. 53–58). The close association of uncleanness with death is shown in 13:45–46. The person afflicted with a serious skin disease behaved as a mourner (“let the hair of his head hang loose”). He was excluded from the camp, not to protect the health of Israel, but because God was in the camp and uncleanness (death) had to be separated from the presence of God (life). See Num. 5:1–4; 12:14, 15.

These ceremonies conducted by the priest do not cure skin disease. A diseased person comes to the priest after he has been healed (Luke 5:14). The task of the priest is to make ceremonially clean the person who, due to his uncleanness, has been excluded from the camp, from his people, and from God. Through these ceremonial cleansings, which take place in two stages a week apart, the diseased individual is restored to fellowship with God and with His people.

The first stage of cleansing takes place outside the camp. The man washes himself and his clothes, and he shaves. Two birds are taken. The blood of one is used to purify the man. The death of that bird portrays the end of the man’s old life outside the camp, and the flight to freedom of the other pictures his liberation from the effects of the disease. Then, the man can enter the camp again.

In the second cleansing stage, the Israelite is brought back into full communion with God. The ceremonies here resemble the consecration of the priest (ch. 8). The Israelite is daubed with blood and anointed with oil, being linked to the altar, the symbol of God’s presence. A variation on this restoration procedure is prescribed for the poor in vv. 21–31.

This passage adapts principles of diagnosis (13:47–58) and cleansing (14:1–7) to the problem of “disease” (mildew or dry rot) in houses. This problem would have arisen after the settlement in Canaan (v. 34).

This chapter deals with the uncleanness caused by discharges from the sexual organs: (a) long-term male discharge (e.g., gonorrhea; vv. 2–15); (b) short-term male discharges (vv. 16–18); (c) short-term female discharge (menstruation; vv. 19–24); and (d) long-term female discharges (vv. 25–30). That perfectly natural processes like sexual intercourse (v. 18) or menstruation should make someone unclean (i.e., unfit to worship) is surprising. But all these cases involve the loss of bodily fluids (blood or semen), and any loss of a “life fluid” suggested death and was incompatible with the presence of God, who is perfect life.

The NT shows God, the giver of perfect life, incarnate in Jesus Christ, healing those who suffered exclusion from His presence under these OT rules (Matt. 9:20–22). The divine program of redemption was historically progressive. The old covenant arrangements that seem so strange to us were early object lessons, a “guardian” pointing forward to the full redemption accomplished in Jesus Christ (Gal. 3:24, 25).

The Day of Atonement, when annual atonement is made for the sins of the nation, is the holiest day in the OT calendar. It falls in the seventh month of the Hebrew calendar (September/October) and involves the offering of various sacrifices, the entry of the high priest into the Most Holy Place (in this chapter referred to simply as the “Holy Place” or “holy sanctuary”), and the dispatch of a goat into the wilderness carrying the people’s sins. For a summary of the sacrifices, see notes on chs. 1; 4; and 5. A summary of the rites is given in vv. 6–10 and fuller details in vv. 11–28. The Day of Atonement proceeds according to the following steps: (a) The high priest washes and dresses (v. 4); (b) he sacrifices a bull as a sin offering for himself (v. 6; cf. v. 11); (c) he enters the Most Holy Place and sprinkles the ark with blood (vv. 12–14); (d) he takes two goats and by lot chooses one to be the scapegoat (Azazel) and the other to be a sin or purification offering (vv. 7, 8); (e) he sacrifices one goat as a sin or purification offering (vv. 9, 15); (f) he enters the Most Holy Place and sprinkles the ark with blood (v. 15); (g) he goes out to the outer part of the tabernacle of meeting and sprinkles the blood (v. 16); (h) he goes out into the courtyard of the tabernacle and sprinkles the main altar with blood (vv. 18, 19); (i) he confesses the sins of the Israelites as he lays his hands on the scapegoat’s head (v. 21); (j) he sends the scapegoat into the wilderness (vv. 21, 22); (k) the scapegoat gone, the high priest changes into his regular garments and washes (vv. 23, 24); and (l) finally, he offers burnt offerings for himself and for the people (vv. 24, 25).

For the high priest, the most important aspects of the ceremony are his entry into the Most Holy Place with the blood of the sin or purification offering and the dispatch of the scapegoat into the wilderness. These actions atone for the sins of repentant Israelites (vv. 16, 19, 21, 22). All sin offerings serve to cleanse both the earthly sanctuary and the worshipers, but on other occasions the high priest does not enter the (inner) Most Holy Place, but only the anteroom before the separating veil (usually called the “Holy Place”), the chamber containing the altar of incense, the gold lampstand, and the table of showbread. Because the ark of the covenant, the focal point of God’s presence in the tabernacle (v. 2 note; Ex. 25:17–22 and notes), is housed in the Most Holy Place, entry to the Most Holy Place is rare and dangerous (v. 2). That the high priest enters the inner chamber only on this one day of the year indicates the depth of atonement being made.

The scapegoat ceremony was also unique to this day. By placing his hands on the goat’s head and confessing the nation’s sins, the high priest transfers those sins to the goat. The goat then symbolically carries the people’s sins away into the wilderness. Christians have long regarded the scapegoat as a type of Christ. That Christ was delivered to the Gentiles and killed outside the walls of Jerusalem indicates that He was sent “outside the camp” like the scapegoat of old (Heb. 9:6–28; 13:11–13).

**16:1 death of the two sons of Aaron.** See 10:1–3.

Lit. “atonement covering” or “place of atonement” (Ex. 25:17 note). This slab of pure gold serves as a lid for the ark and as a base for the two golden cherubim. The divine presence appears above the lid of the ark (Ex. 25:22; Ps. 99:1), and Aaron sprinkles the mercy seat with blood on the Day of Atonement. God symbolically reveals the gospel through this cover on the ark. The ark contains the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments inscribed by the finger of God Himself, representing the principal obligations of the Sinai covenant (Deut. 10:1–5). Since all humans have violated God’s moral demands, the righteousness of God demands death (Ezek. 18:20; Rom. 6:23). God provides the only means of atonement for His chosen people and for their reconciliation to Him—the atoning blood on the ark’s cover. That blood-drenched cover is the meeting point of the holy God with His unholy people. It resembles the heavenly sanctuary where Christ has entered with His own blood (Heb. 9:12), blood that is efficacious for all the sins—past, present, and future—of His people (Rom. 3:21–26; Heb. 9:15).

Before offering a goat for the people, Aaron is to offer a bull as a sin or purification offering and a ram as a burnt offering for himself and his family (v. 5). By contrast, Jesus Christ, the Mediator of the eternal new covenant, is without sin and therefore offered sacrifice for His people only (Heb. 7:26, 27).
LORD **.** The goat to be sacrificed.

The smoke from the incense serves as a screen between the mercy seat and the high priest, probably to prevent the high priest from seeing the divine presence (v. 13; cf. Ex. 33:20). It also may serve to avert God’s wrath (Num. 16:46–50).

Here the term denotes the Most Holy Place, or inner sanctuary. The object of the sacrificial ritual is the sanctuary itself, which was defiled by people’s sins. The earthly sanctuary is a representation of the heavenly sanctuary that the blood of Christ also cleansed (Heb. 9:23, 24).

**which dwells with them.** Lit. “which camps among them.” The verb connotes impermanence. God’s presence is not finalized in this arrangement. His tent dwelling foreshadowed His dwelling among His people through Christ’s incarnation (John 1:14). Today He has sent His Spirit upon His new covenant people, the church (Acts 2), and His Spirit indwells believers, making them the temple of God (1 Cor. 3:16; 6:19; Eph. 2:21, 22). His final dwelling with His people will occur in the new heavens and the new earth (Rev. 21:1–4).

See text note. The ordinary Israelites are to show penitence for their sins by not working, by fasting, and possibly by wearing sackcloth (Ps. 69:10, 11). Failing to observe the Day of Atonement could entail death (23:28–30). This is the only holy day to which this threat is attached.
By contrast, Jesus Christ offered the final and complete sacrifice for sin (Heb. 9:23–28).

In these chapters, the Lord’s demands for holiness clearly reach into every aspect of Israel’s life. In a discussion on topics as diverse as sexual behavior and the Year of Jubilee, capital crimes, and the tabernacle loaves, the Lord teaches that Israel must reflect His holiness in their behavior.

In the wilderness period, animals could be killed only at the tabernacle, even for ordinary meals. This was to prevent secret sacrifices to idols (v. 7). After entering Canaan, this rule was relaxed (Deut. 12:15–16).

Or, has committed a transgression as grievous as any involving bloodshed.

**cut off.** See note on 7:20.

One of the most important theological statements in Leviticus (see also Lev. 18:5). Life is sacred because it belongs to God. As a mark of respect for life and for its Creator, no Israelite may eat meat with blood in it “for the life of the flesh is in the blood” (cf. Gen. 9:4–6). A second reason is that it is the blood that makes “atonement for your souls.” The animal’s life, represented by its blood shed in sacrifice, takes the place of the life of the worshiper, symbolically redeeming him. Because animal blood is the sign of salvation, people may not consume it. These ideas are both assumed and transformed in the NT. Christ’s shed blood actually atoned for sin (Heb. 9:14, 22; 1 John 1:7), and those who drink that blood spiritually—receiving the benefits of His death through faith in Him alone—have eternal life (John 6:54).

**have given it for you.** The sacrificial system of the OT is God’s gracious gift to His people to enable them to live in God’s presence. In anticipation of the final and perfect blood sacrifice offered by Christ, God Himself ordains the procedures whereby His righteous wrath might be averted and His people reconciled to Him.

Moses instructs Israel concerning unlawful practices linked to sex and family, including incest (vv. 6–20), child sacrifice (v. 21), homosexuality (v. 22), and bestiality (v. 23). Israel’s neighbors were much less restrained in their sexual attitudes and behavior (v. 3). They permitted closer intermarriage than allowed here; they allowed homosexuality (cf. v. 22), and even some types of bestiality (cf. v. 23). The regulations in this chapter presuppose that an Israelite would normally marry another Israelite. However, unions between blood relatives of the first degree (brother-sister, father-daughter) and the second degree (father-granddaughter, nephew-aunt) were prohibited. Marriage between close relatives by marriage was also banned.

**You shall therefore keep my statutes and my rules.** The passage is one of only two passages from Leviticus that the apostle Paul quotes (cf. Gal 3:12ff. and Rom 10:5ff.). This command expresses in a single sentence the goal and rationale of the law, which requires perfect, personal, and perpetual obedience from all people.

Not one’s own mother (cf. v. 7), but the father’s second wife (cf. 1 Cor. 5:1). The phrase “it is your father’s nakedness” recalls the teaching in Gen. 2:24 that the married couple “become one flesh.”
A full sister or half sister.
A stepsister.

The law of levirate marriage (Deut. 25:5 note) encouraged a man to marry his widowed sister-in-law if her first marriage was childless. This provision shows the importance of preserving the family inheritance by perpetuating the family line in OT society (Num. 27:1–11 note).
The daughter of the woman would be the man’s stepdaughter or step-granddaughter.
The sad example of Jacob’s marriage to Leah and Rachel illustrates the compassionate wisdom of this law (Gen. 29:23–30:24).
See note on ch. 15.

The custom of sacrificing children was practiced among the ancient Phoenicians and pagan inhabitants of Canaan (Deut. 12:31 note). The cult of Molech, a god of the Ammonites, was a temptation to the Israelites (cf. 1 Kin. 11:7; 2 Kin. 23:10).

Ritual uncleanness, caused by sin, was contagious—all and everything that came in contact with it was infected, including the sanctuary (16:16 note) and the land. The pollution of the land by impurity was seen as a grave danger and a major threat to Israel. Though the Israelites would be given the privilege of occupying the Promised Land, the land would “vomit” them out if they were to defile it as the previous inhabitants had.

**vomited.** This personification of the land underscores the poisonous contagion of uncleanness due to sin.

verse_quote: cut off from among their people.
note: See note on 7:20. God requires personal, entire, exact, and perpetual obedience of both corporate Israel and individuals who reside within her.

The instruction here repeats many of the same points of chs. 18 and 19 (for parallel verses, consult the cross-references), but with the addition of prescribed penalties. The death penalty is indicated for many offenses, pointing to the horror with which God viewed them (cf. Rom. 1:18–32). In other cases, divine penalties, such as cutting off (7:20 note), are mentioned; these cover situations where detection might be difficult (v. 18) or family solidarity might make the head of the family reluctant to punish the offender (v. 17).

Ceremonial cleanliness regulations specific to the priests are recorded. These deal with priests in general (vv. 1–9), the high priest (vv. 10–15), and priests suffering from defects (vv. 16–24). All priests who serve within the tabernacle have to show God’s holiness in their character and in their bodies. Because their duties bring them closer to God, it is essential that they be holy. Holiness in restored man ultimately involves his perfection and health (fullness of life; freedom from mortality and decay), so priests with certain handicaps are forbidden to offer sacrifice (vv. 17–21). Wholeness is closely associated with holiness. But handicapped priests still enjoy a full share of priestly provisions (v. 22).

**21:1** Holiness (as a key attribute of God, who is Himself life) and death are incompatible; therefore, priests may not mourn for any save their closest relatives (vv. 2–3).
Mourning customs involving disfigurement of the body were also banned, for priests as holy men had to have whole bodies (Deut. 14:1 note).
The high priest, who has the privilege of entering into God’s immediate presence, is obliged to avoid all contact with death (cf. 10:6, 7).
For any unclean person to eat holy food from a sacrifice is to risk death (7:20–21). Uncleanness (death) and holiness (life) are not to mix.
These verses define which dependents of the priests are allowed to eat sacrificial food.
A penalty of restitution is prescribed for non-priests who eat the priestly portions of the sacrifices (cf. 5:14–16).

Only blemish-free animals are to be sacrificed. This is partly because God is not to be given anything but the best (Mal. 1:8), and partly because the holiness of sacrifices is symbolized by a perfect physical body (cf. 21:17–21).
The freewill offering is optional and not strictly mandated by God; therefore, minor blemishes may be tolerated.

note: This action was taken to rid themselves of the guilt they had contracted by hearing his blasphemy.

verse_quote: eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
note: Designed to curb exaggerated revenge (cf. Gen. 4:24), this formula vividly expressed the principle that punishment should be proportionate to the offense. It seems not to have been enforced literally (see Ex. 21:26, 27; Deut. 19:21 note). Jesus’ opposition to the use of this phrase in everyday relationships and not in court cases for which it was intended was not an abrogation of the principle of equivalence (cf. Matt. 5:38–42). God never intended the rule to be strictly enforced in the normal course of everyday problems and disagreements, but gave it as a legal principle of restitution. Jesus calls for viewing this principle in light of its original intent for use in a court setting, as well as in light of the love commandment (19:18; cf. Matt. 7:12), in the interests of the kingdom (Matt. 5:10–12), and in the knowledge of God’s coming wrath (Rom. 12:17–21; cf. Deut. 32:35).

The Lord demonstrates His ownership of the Promised Land through laws preventing the exploitation of the land and its tenants (v. 23 note).

**25:1–7** Just as humans need a day of rest, land without fertilizers needs to lie fallow for a time. See the similar regulations in Ex. 23:10, 11.

More than a fallow year, this was a year in which all the poor who had fallen into debt were given a fresh start. Loans were written off. Land that had been sold was returned to its original owner, and slaves were released (v. 40).

God protected His gift to each family within the covenant community. In this way He protected the family structure, provided life in perpetuity for them, and prevented unrestrained commercial exploitation of His gift.

Although God gave Israel the land as one of His good gifts to them to be enjoyed (Deut. 6:10–12; 8:10–13), He still retained final ownership and could terminate the lease should the people prove undesirable tenants. They did not possess the land as an inalienable right but within the structures of a covenantal relationship with God. The land was not property over which the Israelites had total and final control. It symbolized life with God.
All the sales described here took place because of hardship. Land was not to be permanently sold from one family to another.
It was hoped that a relative would buy a poor man’s land and return it to him. In any event, he or his family would receive it back in the Year of Jubilee.
In contrast to agricultural land, houses within cities had to be redeemed within a year or the sale was permanent., 30
See note on Deut. 23:19 (Ps. 15:5).

If a man sold a son or a daughter into slavery because of debt, the slave was released after seven years (Ex. 21:2–11; Deut. 15:12–18). This text deals with an even worse debt where, presumably after selling his land for a sum insufficient to pay the debt, a man and his whole family were sold as slaves (v. 41). In such a case they were released in the Year of Jubilee.
The Lord’s instruction to the Israelites culminates in promises of blessings for obedience (vv. 3–13) and of curses for disobedience (vv. 14–39).

Israel’s obedience to the covenant requirements would be rewarded with blessing (Ex. 20:12; Deut. 28:1–14; cf. Matt. 6:4), culminating in the greatest of all blessings—the presence of God with His people (see Ex. 29:42–46 and note).

Disobedience to God brings suffering (Ex. 20:7; Deut. 28:15–68). Many prophetic passages echo Lev. 26 and Deut. 28, as the prophets argued that the people were suffering—or were about to suffer—God’s anger over their sins.

Even in judgment there was always hope (Deut. 30:1–10). Punishment did not mean an end to the covenant (vv. 44, 45; Gen. 17:2 note; Rom. 11:1–29). God’s judgments on His people proved He still cared about them (Heb. 12:5, 6).
A summary conclusion to the variety of instructional material in chs. 1–26. The Hebrew term “laws” refers to teaching or instruction and not legislation.

The final chapter of Leviticus deals with gifts promised to God, probably by Israelites in dire distress when they made a vow. Later, they might wish to take back the property vowed. The provisions of this chapter showed when and how this could be done.

It was possible to offer oneself or a member of one’s family to the full-time service of God in the temple (1 Sam. 1:11). But only Levites could serve God as temple priests; other vowed persons had to be redeemed according to the tariff described in vv. 3–8.
Sacrificial animals could not be withdrawn once vowed.
Non-sacrificial animals had to be redeemed.

Property and persons devoted to God (i.e., placed under the ban) were irrevocably to be placed in the service of God (v. 28), or utterly destroyed (v. 29). This solemn vow was probably pronounced by national leaders, often in time of war (Num. 21:2; 1 Sam. 15), or against those practicing idolatry (Deut. 13:16; 20:17 note).
A tenth of agricultural produce was given to God (i.e., to the priestly tribe of Levi, see Num. 18:21–29; Deut. 12:6–18; 14:22–29 and notes).
